OPPOSITION OF DEFENDANTS KATIE HALL, ESQ. &
THE NATIONAL CENTER FOR MISSING & EXPLOITED CHILDREN
TO PLAINTIFF'S MOTION FOR LEAVE TO FILE SECOND AMENDED COMPLAINT
Defendants Katie Hall, Esq. and The National Center for Missing & Exploited Children
[collectively, "NCMEC"], by and through undersigned counsel and pursuant to the Rules and
Orders of this Honorable Court, hereby respectfully oppose Plaintiff's second Motion for Leave
to File a Second Amended Complaint [Doc. 114]. The Motion for Leave should be denied on the
basis of futility. In further support, NCMEC states as follows:
I.
FACTUAL SETTING/PROCEDURAL POSTURE
The subject Motion represents Plaintiff's sixth effort to state a claim as to NCMEC,
whether by original pleading or attempts to amend his Complaint as to the dispute in question.
In the original lawsuit filed by Plaintiff in this matter —Ballentine v. NCMEC, Case No. 1:26-ev-
01341 (E.D. Va.) Plaintiff filed his original complaint on May 19, 2026. After NCMEC moved
to dismiss the complaint, Plaintiff filed a motion for leave to file an amended complaint on July
27, 2026, which motion was opposed by NCMEC. Two days later, on July 29, 2026, Plaintiff

voluntarily dismissed the lawsuit (presumably to avoid the potential that he would not be granted
leave to amend).
The following day, Plaintiff filed the original complaint in this matter. [Doc. 1].
Approximately one week later, Plaintiff filed a First Amended Complaint. [Doc. 5]. On August
20, 2026, Plaintiff filed a motion seeking leave to file a Supplemental Complaint. [Doc. 28].
(Plaintiff later withdrew that request.) On September 8, 2026, Plaintiff filed a Motion for Leave
to File Second Amended and Supplemental Complaint. [Doc. 59]. The Court ordered Plaintiff
to file a redlined version of the proposed pleading on September 9, 2026. [Doc. 64]. Plaintiff
refused to comply with the September 9 Order, instead filing objections [Doc. 66] and a motion
to set aside the Order. [Doc. 67]. On October 7, 2026, the Court denied Plaintiff's original
motion for leave to file a second amended complaint, noting that "Plaintiff was given ample
opportunity to comply with the Court's September 9, 2026 Order... but has failed to do so."
Plaintiff's asserts that his proposed Second Amended Complaint seeks to add NCMEC's
chief legal officer-—Ms. Yiota Souras, Esq.— as a named defendant. Doc. 114 at 10. The
pleading does not add any additional causes of action. Id. at 9| 11. Other than seeking to add Ms.
Souras as a defendant, Plaintiff asserts that the pleading is intended to (a) plead facts concerning
Ms. Souras' responsibilities and her role in the events at issue; (b) plead "facts concerning
Plaintiff's legal name and Plaintiff's Meta accounts and, on information and belief, the contents
of the two CyberTipline reports [at issue]..." and (c) "facts concerning the letters' wording,
omitted limitations, and the meaning a reasonable reader would take from them." Id. at 9 12.!
' While the redlined version of the proposed Second Amended Complaint contains significantly more
hanges, the majority appear to be relatively minor, such as changing "states" to "disclosed" and "havin
ndergone" to "undergoing " et

As to Ms. Souras, while the majority of the alleged facts are asserted "upon information
and belief," the new allegations appear to relate to Ms. Souras' role as Chief Legal Officer at
NCMEC, and to the fact that she was employed as an associate at Orrick, Herrington & Sutcliffe
LLP more than twenty years prior. See Doc. 114 at Ex. B, pp. 17-20. (That firm represents co-
defendant Meta Platforms, Inc. in this matter.) Otherwise, the allegations effectively repeat the
allegations made as to Ms. Hall relating to the transmission of the letters in question.
As to the facts "concerning Plaintiff's legal name [etc.]," these new allegations contain
further reference to Plaintiff's legal name, that he never used his legal name as a username or to
set up a Meta-owned platform, etc. Id. at pp. 33-34.
As to the final asserted substantive changes, they include noting that NCMEC's response
indicated a period of "July 1, 2022 through the date of compliance," while the letters stated "July
1, 2022 and the present"; alleging that the Schedule requested "CyberTipline report, referral or
submission," while the responsive letters referred to "CyberTipline reports"; and that the letters
listed the search terms utilized in the same order in which they were submitted by Plaintiff. Id. at
pp. 20.
Plaintiff does not add any causes of action, but continues to seek $42,820,260.00 (Forty-
Two Million Eight Hundred and Twenty Thousand Two Hundred and Sixty Dollars) in damages.
II.
STANDARD OF REVIEW
Under Rule 15(a), leave to amend is to be granted freely, "absent bad faith, undue
prejudice to the opposing party, or futility of amendment." Hardee v. Mun. Jail Va. Beach
Sheriff's Off., 2025 U.S. Dist. LEXIS 184735, *5 (E.D. Va. 2025) (quoting United States v.
Pittman, 209 F.3d 314, 317 (4th Cir. 2000)); Save Our Sound OBX, Inc. v. N.C. DOT, 914 F.3d
213, 228 (4th Cir. 2019) (same). A proposed amendment is futile "when it is clearly insufficient
3

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-WEF Document 139
1674
Filed 11/10/26 Page 4 of 8 PagelD#
or frivolous on its face... [or] if the claim it presents would not survive a motion to dismiss."
Id.; United States ex rel. Wilson v. Kellogg Brown & Root, Inc., 525 F.3d 370, 375 (4th Cir.
2008). In determining futility, the Court is empowered to "apply common sense." Nasim v.
Warden, Md. House of Corr., 64 F.3d 951, 954 (4th Cir. 1995).
III.
ARGUMENT
NCMEC respectfully submits that leave to amend at this stage would be futile and
unnecessary, as both NCMEC and co-defendant Meta Platforms, Inc. have motions to dismiss
pending, which have been fully briefed by all interested parties to the respective motions. None
of the additional factual allegations appear to have any impact on the arguments raised in
NCMEC's pending motions to dismiss, thus rendering amendment futile at present.? (That is not
to suggest that NCMEC presumes to predict how the Court will rule on its pending Motions to
Dismiss; only that further amendment at present would not impact the arguments raised in the
Motions.)
First, NCMEC argues that Counts I, II, III, and VI are barred by the litigation privilege.
The facts desired to be added do not impact those arguments whatsoever, as NCMEC contends
that it is (at a minimum) shielded from Plaintiff's defamation and intentional infliction of
emotional distress claims by that privilege. Ms. Souras, as NCMEC's Chief Legal Officer,
would similarly enjoy that privilege, to the extent this Court determines it to be applicable.
Second, NCMEC asserts that NCMEC (including Ms. Hall) enjoy qualified immunity as
to Counts I, II, and V (if not all counts), pursuant to 18 U.S.C. § 2258D and 34 U.S.C. § 20505.
As briefed in support of NCMEC's Motions to Dismiss, 18 U.S.C. § 2258D provides immunity
to NCMEC, as well as "any director, officer, employee, or agent of NCMEC, arising from the
2 The desired addition of Ms. Souras as a defendant would not impact those arguments, either.
4

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-WEF Document 139
1675
Filed 11/10/26 Page 5 of 8 PagelD#
performance of any CyberTipline responsibilities or functions of NCMEC..." 18 U.S.C. §
2258D(a). Similarly, 34 U.S.C. § 20505 provides for immunity from defamation, libel, slander,
etc.—in the absence of actual malice, or action taken unrelated to an activity mandated by
federal law— for NCMEC, "including any of its officers, employees, or agents..." As such, the
inclusion of Ms. Souras (as NCMEC's Chief Legal Officer) would not impact this basis for
dismissal, either, nor does it appear that any additional factual allegations would have any impact
on the Court's analysis, either.
Third, NCMEC has asserted that the allegedly-defamatory statements are true, and thus
not actionable. Plaintiff has not plausibly alleged that the allegedly-defamatory statements in
question are not, in fact, true, because Plaintiff does not have access to those statements. (Given
the sensitive nature of NCMEC's CyberTipline work, and the need to encourage reporting of
suspected instances of child exploitation without fear of retaliatory lawsuits, there is obviously
good reason these are not publicly-available documents.) While Plaintiff has asserted that he has
not engaged in any conduct constituting a violation of any law that would give rise to a
meritorious CyberTipline report, that is not the issue; the issue is whether NCMEC received such
a report, and Plaintiff cannot plausibly assert that is untrue. No additional factual allegations, nor
the attempted inclusion of Ms. Souras, can change that.
Fourth, NCMEC has argued that the allegedly-defamatory meaning cannot reasonably be
imputed from the language in NCMEC's responsive letters to Plaintiff (which, as noted in the
Motions to Dismiss, is a question of law). NCMEC is not alleged to have stated that Plaintiff
engaged in reportable conduct, nor does NCMEC take that position. NCMEC is alleged to have
stated that it received two CyberTipline reports based on the search terms requested by Plaintiff.
The proposed amended pleading does not impact this argument, either; what Plaintiff requested,
5

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-WEF Document 139
1676
Filed 11/10/26 Page 6 of 8 PagelD#
and how NCMEC responded, are spelled out in black and white, and not susceptible to additional
factual allegations. Further, the proposed amended pleading does not establish or allow for a
reasonable inference that NCMEC's statements not only imparted false innuendo, but also that
NCMEC intended or endorsed the false innuendo. See, e.g., Chapin v. Knight-Ridder, Inc., 993
F.2d 1087, 1092 (4th Cir. 1993).
Fifth, NCMEC has asserted that Plaintiff's claims for Intentional Infliction of Emotional
Distress also fail on the grounds that Plainti ff cannot plausibly assert that NCMEC's action of
responding to subpoenas mailed to NCMEC by Plaintiff was "intentional or reckless," nor that
NCMEC's conduct was "so outrageous in character, and so extreme in degree, as to go beyond
all possible bounds of decency, and to be regarded as atrocious, and utterly intolerable in a
civilized community..." Russo v. White, 241 Va. 23, 27 (1991). Plaintiffs' proposed amended
complaint does not impact that analysis, either.
Finally, NCMEC asserts that Plaintiff's conspiracy counts-Counts IV and V-fail, as
they are predicated entirely on conclusory allegations with no factual support whatsoever.
Presumably, Plaintiff believes that the allegation that Ms. Souras worked as an associate for the
firm representing co-defendant Meta Platforms, Inc.—approximately 20 years ago-- informs
these conspiracy counts. NCMEC respectfully submits that does not. Orrick maintains
numerous offices throughout North America, Europe, China, Singapore, Japan, etc., and has
presumably employed many thousands of attorneys over the past 20 years. See, e.g.,
orrick.com/en/Locations. No other additional facts asserted appear to relate to Plaintiff's
conclusory assertions as to the existence and operation of the alleged conspiracy or conspiracies.
6

IV.
CONCLUSION
As noted, NCMEC does not presume to know how the Court will rule on the pending
motions to dismiss. However, in the event that NCMEC's motions to dismiss are granted in full,
that would be dispositive of all of Plaintiff's claims as to NCMEC, and would also be dispositive
of any claims that could be asserted as to Ms. Souras. Given that Plaintiff has previously
amended his Complaint, and the proposed modifications to the First Amended Complaint would
not disturb successful dismissal arguments by NCMEC, NCMEC respectfully requests that this
Honorable Court deny Plaintiff's Motion for Leave to Amend, or in the alternative hold the
motion in abeyance until the Court ascertains whether Plaintiff is able to state any claim upon
which relief may be granted as to NCMEC.
Respectfully submitted,
